group.passage: Not long ago, the night train seemed headed for the history books. In 2013 and 2014 alone, overnight services linking cities such as Paris and Madrid, Berlin and Paris, and Amsterdam and Prague were cut. Budget airlines, high-speed daytime trains and long-distance buses had taken away many of their passengers, and rail companies were reluctant to invest in replacing their aging carriages. Night trains are also expensive to operate. They require special sleeping cars, and each train can usually make only one journey a day. Since hardly anyone wants to board or leave a train at two o'clock in the morning, the stations along the way bring in little extra income. When Germany's national railway abandoned many of its overnight routes, Austria's national railway, ÖBB, took over several of them, including the line from Munich to Rome. Then attitudes began to shift. A movement known in Swedish as flygskam, or "flight shame," spread from Scandinavia, urging travelers to avoid flying whenever possible. In Sweden, domestic air travel fell by 9 percent in 2018. The European Union declared 2021 the European Year of Rail, and new overnight routes and modern sleeping cars have since appeared across the continent. Their appeal is easy to understand: passengers can board after dinner, sleep in a proper bed and wake up in another country, without the stress of an early-morning flight. The table helps explain why climate-conscious travelers are interested. For every kilometer a passenger travels, a domestic flight is responsible for about 246 grams of greenhouse gases, while an average train trip in the United Kingdom produces about 35 grams. Yet the night train still faces an uncertain future. On busy routes, sleeper fares rise quickly and can be hard to afford, and buying and approving new sleeping cars is slow and costly. If night trains are to become a true alternative to flying, supporters argue, they must become cheaper as well as greener.

translation_zh.text:
歐洲夜車的復興

不久以前，夜車似乎就要走入歷史。光是在 2013 和 2014 年，連接巴黎與馬德里、柏林與巴黎、阿姆斯特丹與布拉格等城市的夜間列車就被裁撤了。廉價航空、高速日間列車和長途巴士搶走了它們許多乘客，鐵路公司也不願意花錢汰換老舊的車廂。

夜車的營運成本也很高。它們需要特殊的臥鋪車廂，而且每列車通常一天只能跑一趟。由於幾乎沒有人想在凌晨兩點上下車，沿途各站帶來的額外收入很少。當德國國鐵放棄許多夜間路線時，奧地利國鐵 ÖBB 接手了其中幾條，包括從慕尼黑到羅馬的路線。

接著，人們的態度開始轉變。一個瑞典語稱為 flygskam、也就是「飛行羞恥」的運動從北歐擴散開來，呼籲旅客盡可能不要搭飛機。在瑞典，國內航空旅行在 2018 年減少了 9%。歐盟把 2021 年定為「歐洲鐵路年」，此後新的夜間路線和現代化的臥鋪車廂陸續在歐洲各地出現。它們的吸引力不難理解：乘客可以吃完晚餐再上車，睡在真正的床上，醒來時已到了另一個國家，而且沒有趕清晨班機的壓力。

表格有助於說明為什麼在意氣候的旅客對夜車感興趣。每位乘客每移動一公里，國內航班要為約 246 公克的溫室氣體負責，而英國一般的火車旅程只產生約 35 公克。然而，夜車的未來仍然不確定。在熱門路線上，臥鋪票價漲得很快，可能讓人難以負擔，而購買與審核新的臥鋪車廂既緩慢又昂貴。支持者主張，如果夜車要成為飛行的真正替代方案，它們必須在更環保的同時，也變得更便宜。
